en: The Sūtra on the Eight Virtues of the Ocean, spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Anabhibhūta. At that time, he was by the side of a river, constantly [practicing] the ten...
On the fifth day, he preached the Sūtra of Precepts for the śramaṇas.
The Buddha sat in profound stillness, remaining silent for a long time.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and said:
“The śramaṇas are seated and settled; they would delight to hear the pure Dharma.
The World-Honored One remained silent.
Ānanda rose three times and said:
"The night is already half spent; the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra may now be recited.
The World-Honored One then said:
"Among the śramaṇas, there are those who are defiled and turbid, whose minds are perverse and whose conduct violates the Dharma, and who transgress the precepts of a śramaṇa."

"Their majestic spiritual power is so profound that it is beyond the capacity of those who are base and lowly to practice; as their purity and defilement are mutually opposed, I did not speak of them.

Then the Venerable Maudgalyāyana entered meditative concentration with a single mind, and with the pure vision of his Dharma-eye, he clearly perceived that there were indeed practices within their minds that could be abandoned.
Maudgalyāyana immediately said to him:
"Arise! This is not a place for you, a worldly man, to sit."
He refused to rise; [the king] pulled him by the arm and led him out, saying:
"You possess no supreme virtue and harbor the six heterodoxies in your heart; how dare you, with this foul and filthy body, sit upon a throne of celestial fragrance?"
"You are a person who has abandoned [the Dharma]; you are no longer a śramaṇa.
Maudgalyāyana immediately returned to his pure seat.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"You are so foolish! You do not understand my parable; it was only when I took you by the arm that you would leave.
The Buddha said to the śramaṇa, "Listen attentively to my words."
The śramaṇas replied, “Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.
“Observe that great ocean; it possesses eight excellent qualities.”
Its breadth is vast and boundless, its depth unfathomable; as one enters it, it becomes increasingly deep without the obstructions encountered before—this is its first virtue.
The ocean tides do not exceed their appointed times; this is its second virtue.
The ocean contains all manner of treasures, embracing everything within its embrace; yet it does not tolerate a putrid corpse, which the divine winds blow to the shore; this is its third virtue.

The ocean harbors a multitude of treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, agate, and divine moon-bright pearls; among its thousands of wonders and myriad marvels, there is nothing one seeks that cannot be obtained. These are its four virtues.
Beneath the heavens, there are five great rivers that flow toward the ocean: those flowing west are named Gaṅgā;
those flowing south are named Sītā;
and those flowing east consist of two rivers:
One is named Śālukī and one is named Airāvatī;
the northern-flowing river is named Mūṣikā.
These five rivers flow forth and all enter the ocean, where they all discard their former names and merge into the sea—this is the virtue of the five.

The five rivers and ten thousand streams, drenched by rain until the end of time, have flowed since the establishment of heaven and earth; though rain falls and rivers pour forth, the waters of the sea remain as they were, neither increasing nor decreasing—this is its sixth virtue.

In the ocean there are many fish of immense and towering bodies. The body of the first fish is four thousand li long; the body of the second fish is eight thousand li long; the body of the third fish is twelve thousand li long; the body of the fourth fish is sixteen thousand li long; the body of the fifth fish is twenty thousand li long; the body of the sixth fish is twenty-four thousand li long; and the body of the seventh fish is twenty-eight thousand li long—these are the seven virtues.
The seawater is uniformly salty, being the same from the periphery to the center; this is its eighth excellence.
For this reason, the sublime and brilliant divine dragons rejoice in it with delight.

"My sutras and wondrous scriptures likewise possess sublime majesty; they are inexhaustible when read, and their meaning grows ever deeper. Neither Brahmā, Māra, nor Śakra can fathom them; they are as vast and far-reaching as the ocean, profoundly deep and difficult to measure."
For this reason, the śramaṇas delight in it; this is the first virtue.

My disciples further exhort one another to recite the sūtras, practice seated meditation, and observe the rites and models without missing their proper times; they are like the tides of the ocean that do not exceed their appointed hour; this is the second virtue.
My Dharma is pure and clean; its intent lies in serene detachment. Once one's needs for food and clothing are provided, one shall not store even the slightest surplus.

If there are śramaṇas whose inclinations are defiled and turbid, they shall be expelled by the Dharma and may not dwell in the temple. Just as the ocean is vast and generous yet does not tolerate a putrid corpse, such is the third virtue.

My Way encompasses all the various scriptures, and their meanings are complete and exhaustive. When a śramaṇa contemplates them deeply, he refines away the defilements of the mind—greed, lust, anger, envy, and the various impurities of ignorance—just as one polishes a mirror until its tarnish is entirely removed; furthermore, by clearing away even the subtlest obscurations, there is nothing that cannot be seen.
First, while sitting alone, reflect upon the source of birth and death throughout the past; there is nothing that you will not come to know.
Second, contemplate how the heavens, the earth, and all things are like illusions: whatever comes together must inevitably part.
Third, always maintain a compassionate heart, pitying those in the world who are deluded and confused, whose actions are inverted, and who do not recognize their own errors.
Fourth, through self-reflection, one both knows the past and illuminates the future, as well as the destinies toward which the souls and spirits of sentient beings must turn.

I have long held that taking mental purity as a precious jewel is the path; when a śramaṇa removes defilement and attains pure conduct, his heart rejoices in it, just as one of bright character delights in the myriad treasures of the ocean—these are the four virtues.

My Way is vast and great, unifying all into one. Whether one belongs to the lineage of kings, brahmins, gentlemen, or the lowly, once they come to become śramaṇas, they all discard their original surnames and become kin through the Way. The wise and the ignorant encourage one another, their hearts like those of brothers. It is just as various streams merge and are called by the single name "sea. For this reason, śramaṇas delight in it; these are its six virtues.

My Way is subtle and wondrous, and its scriptures are profound and deep; when those of superior capacity attain it, they are designated as: first, the Stream-enterer (Srotāpanna); second, the Once-returner (Sakṛdāgāmin); third, the Non-returner (Anāgāmin); and fourth, the Arhat (Arhan).

The Way of the Arhat is one whose mind is pure like a celestial mani-jewel; possessing the virtue of concealing all defilements, they manifest bodies and forms at will, exercising mastery over life and death, abiding for an infinite duration of life without aging or illness—just as there are divine dragons and fish within the great ocean—for these reasons, the śramaṇa delights in it.

My scriptures possess a beauty of meaning like sweet dew; they are unheard of by immortals and sages, and rarely beheld even by Brahmā or Śakra. From antiquity to the present, there is nothing not recorded within them; both the peripheral and the central are equally correct, just as the ocean is uniformly salty throughout. For this reason, śramaṇas delight in them.
"Indeed, those who behold my sutra will all incline their minds toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The ocean possesses eight virtues, and so too does my sutra.
Ānanda rose again, prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and said:
"As the eastern dawn approaches clarity, I pray that you will explain the precepts of gravity.
The World-Honored One said,
"From this day forward, I shall no longer preach the Sūtra of the Precepts of Gravity."
"If they do not comply with the precepts, I fear that the divine thunder and wrathful anger of the deities will befall them; for this reason, I have not recited the Sūtra of Precepts.
From now on, let us further examine and exhort one another, and assemble on the fifteenth day to recite the Sūtra of Precepts."
The bhikṣus rose and paid homage to the Buddha.
According to the text of this *Sūtra on the Eight Virtues of the Ocean*, it is certainly not a translation by Kumārajīva; it appears to be a scripture from the Later Han period.
It is suspected that this was translated by Zhu Falan; it is likely that the original text was lost, and it has been erroneously attributed to Kumārajīva within the canon.
